name: Dunbar's Number
statement: There is a cognitive limit, about 150, on the number of stable relationships one person can maintain.
meaning: Human cognition seems to cap the number of people whose relationships and mutual histories you can actively track at roughly 150 — Robin Dunbar's own gloss is the number of people you could join for a drink uninvited without it being awkward.
mechanism: Across primates, average social group size tracks the relative size of the neocortex; extrapolating the human ratio predicts a group of about 150. Bonding in primates is done by grooming, and grooming time rises with group size — past a point it would eat an impossible share of the day. Dunbar's thesis is that language evolved as a cheaper form of 'grooming' (talk, gossip) that let humans hold larger groups together, but only up to the cognitive ceiling the brain can track.

examples.text: Hutterite farming communities have historically split in two as membership nears 150: beyond that size, they found, informal social pressure stops being enough to hold the group together and formal hierarchy becomes necessary.

The basic functional military unit, the company, has clustered around 150 across many armies and eras, a size at which people can still know one another well enough to coordinate without a thick layer of bureaucracy.

The manufacturer W.L. Gore (of Gore-Tex) is often cited, via Malcolm Gladwell's The Tipping Point, for capping plant headcount near 150 and building a new facility rather than growing one past it: the point where 'everyone knows everyone' breaks down.

variants.name: The concentric layers
variants.text: 150 is one ring in a nested set, each roughly three times the last: about 5 intimates, 15 close friends, 50 friends, 150 meaningful contacts, 500 acquaintances, and 1,500 faces you can put a name to. The inner rings absorb most of your social attention.

whyItMatters: It sets a natural scale for teams, communities, and organisations: below ~150, trust and reputation can hold a group together informally; above it, you need explicit structure, rules, and hierarchy to do the same job. It is a reminder that 'scaling' a community is not free — past a point the way it coheres has to change.

working.lead: Treat 150 as a soft ceiling, not a target
working.text: it marks where informal cohesion strains, not a hard cliff; the useful move is to notice the strain and add structure before it breaks.
communities and teams often work better divided into human-scale units than grown past the point where everyone can still know everyone.

working.lead: Spend your attention on the inner rings
working.text: the layers say most of your social capacity goes to a small core; guard time for it rather than spreading thin across the whole 150.

limits: The number is a central tendency with a very wide error bar, even Dunbar's original 1992 estimate spanned roughly 100 to 230, so treating 150 as an exact constant overstates it. A 2021 re-analysis by Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind, using updated primate data and modern statistics, recovered wildly method-dependent figures (point estimates from the teens to over a hundred, with confidence intervals spanning single digits to the hundreds) and concluded that a specific cognitive limit 'cannot be derived in this manner.' Critics also note that smaller-brained social species sustain complex societies, and that diet and predation may predict primate group size as well as brain size. Whether 150 is a real cognitive constant or a memorable round number is genuinely disputed.
misreadings: It is not a hard cap that switches off at person 151, nor a claim that you can only ever know 150 people. You can recognise thousands. It is an estimate, with a wide confidence interval, of how many active, two-way relationships you can maintain at once, and its status as a fixed number is contested.
origin: Proposed by the British anthropologist Robin Dunbar in a 1992 paper, 'Neocortex size as a constraint on group size in primates' (Journal of Human Evolution), where a regression across primate species extrapolated the human figure to about 150. He developed the language-evolution side of the argument in his 1993 work and his 1996 book Grooming, Gossip, and the Evolution of Language.

sources.text: Dunbar, R.I.M. (1992). "Neocortex size as a constraint on group size in primates." Journal of Human Evolution, 22(6), 469–493.
